subject: ophthalmology
title: Corneal ulcers and keratitis

steps.tx: Bacterial corneal ulcers develop after epithelial breakdown from trauma, contact lens overwear, ocular surface dryness or blepharitis. Patients present with severe pain, photophobia, ciliary injection, greyish stromal infiltrates, and anterior chamber cells. Severe infections produce a sterile **hypopyon** layering purulent exudate inferiorly. Scraping for Gram stain and culture must precede topical therapy with fortified cefazolin and tobramycin or concentrated fluoroquinolones. Contact lens wearers risk virulent Pseudomonas aeruginosa, whose proteoglycanases melt corneal stroma rapidly.
steps.say: Bacterial corneal ulcers typically arise after epithelial breakdown caused by trauma, contact lens wear or chronic ocular surface disease. Patients report intense pain, marked photophobia, red eyes and a grey white stromal infiltrate. In severe cases, inflammatory cells accumulate in the anterior chamber to form a characteristic hypopyon. The clinician must scrape the ulcer margin for microbiological stains and cultures before starting intensive fortified antibiotics. Pseudomonas infections in contact lens users are particularly dangerous because bacterial enzymes can melt corneal stroma rapidly.

steps.tx: Vegetative agricultural trauma frequently causes **fungal ulcers**, predominantly mediated by filamentous species like Fusarium and Aspergillus or yeasts like Candida. Examination reveals dry, raised infiltrates with feathery margins, surrounding satellite lesions, endothelial plaques, and an immune ring. Diagnosis requires fungal hyphae on potassium hydroxide mounts, followed by topical natamycin or voriconazole for weeks. Topical steroids are strictly contraindicated because they accelerate perforation. Acanthamoeba in contact lens wearers using tap water causes excruciating pain, radial perineuritis and ring infiltrates.
steps.say: Corneal trauma from plant material frequently leads to fungal keratitis caused by filamentous organisms like Fusarium and Aspergillus. Slit lamp examination shows a dry, elevated greyish lesion with feathery borders, satellite infiltrates and stubborn hypopyon. Treatment requires prolonged topical antifungal drops, such as natamycin or voriconazole, while topical steroids must be avoided because they worsen tissue destruction. Acanthamoeba infection should be suspected in contact lens wearers using tap water who develop severe pain out of proportion to clinical signs.

steps.tx: Epithelial **herpes simplex keratitis** presents with dendritic ulcers exhibiting terminal bulbs, staining brightly with fluorescein under cobalt blue light. Trigeminal ganglion reactivation triggers viral replication, treated with topical aciclovir without steroids, which cause geographic ulcers. Recurrent stromal involvement causes immune disciform keratitis or neurotrophic melting, requiring cautious steroids under antiviral cover. Herpes zoster ophthalmicus affects the trigeminal ophthalmic division; cutaneous vesicles on the nasal tip, termed Hutchinson sign, indicate nasociliary nerve involvement and warn of severe ocular inflammation.
steps.say: Herpes simplex keratitis typically presents with a branching dendritic ulcer that shows swollen terminal bulbs when stained with fluorescein. The condition results from reactivation of dormant virus within the sensory trigeminal ganglion. Topical aciclovir ointment is prescribed, but topical steroids are strictly avoided during active epithelial disease because they cause rapid ulcer enlargement. In herpes zoster ophthalmicus, cutaneous vesicles on the tip of the nose represent Hutchinson sign, which indicates nasociliary involvement and warns of impending intraocular inflammation.

steps.tx: Refractory corneal melting leads to structural failure requiring therapeutic **penetrating keratoplasty**. When stromal destruction exposes the posterior limiting lamina, a transparent descemetocele forms, threatening perforation. Active aqueous leakage creates a shallow anterior chamber and a positive Seidel fluorescein test. Small perforations are sealed with cyanoacrylate tissue adhesive and a bandage contact lens, whereas extensive melting requires full-thickness corneal grafting. Lamellar procedures like deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty preserve healthy host endothelium, while endothelial keratoplasty replaces diseased endothelium in pseudophakic bullous keratopathy.
steps.say: Progressive corneal destruction can lead to severe structural failure requiring emergency tectonic keratoplasty. When stromal melting erodes through nearly the entire cornea, Descemet membrane bulges forward to form a fragile descemetocele. A positive Seidel test shows fluorescein diluted by leaking aqueous humour, confirming active perforation and a flat anterior chamber. Small leaks can be sealed with tissue adhesive and a therapeutic bandage lens, but larger defects require tectonic corneal transplantation. Optical penetrating keratoplasty can replace scarred corneal layers later.

steps.tx: Full-thickness **corneal transplantation** replaces diseased host stroma and endothelium with screened donor tissue secured by radial sutures. Postoperative graft surveillance requires vigilant detection of immune allograft rejection, classically recognized by endothelial precipitates and a migrating linear rejection front termed the Khodadoust line. Acute endothelial rejection constitutes an ophthalmic emergency responsive to intensive topical and systemic corticosteroids. Successful visual restoration demands rigorous eye bank donor screening with specular microscopy, and rapid preservation in storage media following donor death.
steps.say: Full thickness penetrating keratoplasty replaces necrotic or scarred cornea with clear donor tissue sutured into place. Following surgery, clinicians must remain alert for signs of graft rejection, which can develop at any time after the initial weeks. Endothelial rejection presents with ciliary flush, graft oedema, keratic precipitates and the pathognomonic Khodadoust line moving across the donor endothelium. Immediate treatment with intensive topical and systemic steroids can reverse this immune attack and save the graft. Long term graft survival depends on careful eye banking.
